newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada union sees progress in GM Canada talks.
newsitem.headline: Canada union sees progress in GM Canada talks.

text.p: The Canadian Auto Workers union (CAW) said Monday that talks will continue with the Canadian subsidiary of General Motors Corp. after progress was made on the key issue of shifting work to outside companies.

Earlier on Monday CAW President Buzz Hargrove had threatened to call off lower-level talks if sufficient progress was not made in the afternoon on the use of outside suppliers, a practice known as outsourcing.
"This is the first indication that (GM) would reverse decisions on outsourcing that they have already made and put in place," Hargrove told reporters during a break in bargaining.
GM Canada spokesman Stew Low agreed some progress had been made in afternoon talks.
"I think (the word) reverse is probably pretty strong," he said. "(But) I think there is some light at the end of the tunnel."
Hargrove declined to give details of the progress, but said he felt more optimistic a deal could be reached before the midnight Wednesday strike deadline.
Hargrove had been pressing the company to reverse decisions to sell two plants in Canada and shift work to outside companies at a total cost of about 5,500 jobs.

"We had a good discussion about a possible solution to those issues," said Hargrove. "I don't want to give anyone false hope, but it is... a significant shift in the position that General Motors has held up until four o'clock this afternoon on these very crucial issues."
The union chose GM Canada one week ago as its second negotiating target after reaching agreement with Chrysler Corp.'s Canadian unit earlier this month.
The Chrysler pact, ratified last weekend, halts plant sales and closings during the three-year agreement and commits Chrysler to replace any union jobs lost due to work done by outside contractors.

At the heart of the disagreement is the CAW's determination to apply the Chrysler deal on outsourcing, which would reverse GM Canada's intentions to sell its Windsor, Ontario, trim plant and Oshawa, Ontario, fabrication plant and contract out other union jobs.
"Before we leave the bargaining table we are going to have the Chrysler pattern on outsourcing language," Hargrove said.

By Monday, talks had endured a bomb threat at one of GM's plants, a secret buyer for two Canadian plants, a letter on outsourcing to employees from GM Canada's president and an argument from the union that GM Canada has already shed nearly as many jobs in the last 10 years as exist in total at Ford Motor Co.'s Canadian unit.

Hargove said the union has approved an escalating strike strategy that would close down G.M. operations in Oshawa and St. Therese, Quebec. He said members will walk out of G.M.'s St. Catharines plant on Oct. 6 and close down remaining plants in London and Windsor, Ontario, on Oct. 9.

Neither the company nor the union would speculate on the cost of a strike. But analysts said last week that a strike could cost General Motors as much as $150 million a week, halt production of some vehicle models and interrupt U.S. operations.

"A long strike might get to the point where it would be reducing G.M.'s profits by maybe $100 million to $150 million a week," said Dave Healy, analyst at Burnham Securities Inc. "It could spread south of the (Canada/U.S.) border as well."
However, the United Auto Workers union, which reached a tentative agreement with Chrysler and has ratified a deal with Ford, must now turn to GM in the next couple of weeks.

Hargrove admitted that a UAW strike deadline at GM in the United States would effectively put a halt to Canadian bargaining, but said he had assurances from UAW President Stephen Yokich that would not happen.
"He assured me that will not happen," Hargrove said. "He will not do anything that will interfere with our bargaining."

Earlier this year United Auto Workers union members at a Dayton, Ohio, brake plant walked off the job over outsourcing. The strike lasted 17 days, shut virtually all GM's North American operations and cost the carmaker about $900 million over 17 days.

The CAW's $36.7 million strike fund may make it tough to carry out a long-term strike and pay strike benefits to 28,000 members at GM. But Hargrove said last week that the union had called a special strike dues convention for the entire 210,000-member union on Oct. 18 as a contingency.
